Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
List the appropriate indications for hip arthroscopy.
Demonstrate hip arthroscopy positioning and how to establish portals.
Discuss different capsulotomy techniques to access the hip joint.
Describe the steps of diagnostic hip arthroscopy.
Classify labral and articular cartilage pathology.
Recognize and avoid common complications.
Procedure
Indications
The indications for hip arthroscopy are expanding.




NOTES

Common intra-articular indications include femoroacetabular impingement, labral tear, loose
body, septic arthritis, synovitis, and adhesive capsulitis.
Extra-articular conditions include trochanteric bursitis, gluteal and hamstring tendon tears,
and heterotopic bone formation.

Indications
Various hip conditions and injuries are amenable to management via hip arthroscopy.
These include intra-articular pathologies, such as femoroacetabular impingement
syndrome, hip labral tears, loose bodies, synovitis, tumors (ie, pigmented villonodular
synovitis), chondral damage, septic arthritis, and adhesive capsulitis.1 (Resource 1). 
Recently, the indications for hip arthroscopy (or endoscopy) have expanded to include
management of extra-articular hip pathology, including trochanteric bursitis, gluteal
tendon tears, proximal hamstring rupture, iliopsoas tendonitis, and heterotopic bone
formation.2
Contraindications
Contraindications to hip arthroscopy include advanced hip arthritis with joint space narrowing,
joint ankylosis, and other conditions that prevent arthroscopic access to the hip joint.

Contraindications
Ideal patient selection for hip arthroscopy is critical to optimizing outcomes and
minimizing complications. Contraindications include advanced hip arthritis (Tönnis grade
2 or worse), ankylosed hip joint, excessive heterotopic ossification preventing
arthroscopic access, osteonecrosis of the femoral head with collapse, active soft-tissue
infection or open wounds, and severe obesity that precludes access to the hip joint

9/3/26, 4:21 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000587
2/28

because of the length of the surgical instruments.1,2 Hip arthroscopy in isolation also is
contraindicated in patients with moderate to severe hip dysplasia.
Techniques
Preoperative Planning
Routine preoperative planning for hip arthroscopy should include the following:
A thorough physical examination of the hip
AP pelvis, Dunn lateral, and false-profile radiographs to assess for joint space, impingement
and acetabular version and coverage
MRI of the hip, which aids in diagnosing labral tears, cartilage injury or degeneration, and
adjacent muscle and tendon tears

Preoperative Planning
A thorough hip examination is essential in the evaluation of hip pain and determining
whether a patient would benefit from hip arthroscopy. This examination includes
observation of the patient’s gait; single-leg stance; range of motion of the hip with
comparison to the opposite side; strength testing; and special tests, such as flexion,
adduction, internal rotation; flexion, abduction, external rotation; and Scour (labral
stress) tests.3,4 (Resource 2).
Routine imaging includes hip AP, Dunn lateral, and false-profile radiographs5 (Figures 1,
2, and 3). On an AP radiograph, the amount of joint space and Tönnis grade, the
crossover sign, and any osteophytes or soft-tissue abnormalities should be noted.6 The
lateral center-edge angle indicates lateral acetabular coverage of the femoral head. It is
measured on an AP radiograph and normally is between 25° and 40°. A lateral center-
edge angle of less than 25° indicates undercoverage, with a borderline dysplasia
indicated by a lateral center-edge angle of 20° to 25° and hip dysplasia indicated by a
lateral center-edge angle of less than 20°. A lateral center-edge angle greater than 40° is
consistent with a pincer lesion. The Tönnis angle also can be used to assess acetabular
coverage, with a normal angle ranging from 0° to 10°. The anterior center-edge angle

radiograph, and typically is between 25° and 40°. The alpha angle is used to identify
femoral head/neck asphericity and associated cam impingement. The angle is measured
on AP and lateral radiographs, with greater than 50° indicating cam impingement.
Figure 1 AP pelvis radiograph. (Courtesy of Alan L. Zhang, MD, San Francisco, CA.)

MRI aids in the diagnosis of hip labral tears (Figures 4 and 5), loose bodies, and chondral
damage and in the evaluation of the integrity of the surrounding muscles and tendons.
MRI may aid in targeting the location of the pathology and planning whether accessory
portals will be necessary for access. The alpha angle is classically measured on an axial
oblique MRI, with greater than 50° indicating cam impingement (Figure 6).

Patient Positioning
Proper patient positioning for hip arthroscopy is crucial to establish safe access to the joint.
Muscle relaxation and a hip distraction table with a padded perineal post generally are
necessary.
The surgical limb is positioned in gentle traction at 0° of hip adduction and 10° to 15° of hip
internal rotation.
Surgeons should confirm ability to obtain fluoroscopic images before draping.

Patient Positioning
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:21 PM
AAOS | Hip Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000587
7/28

Hip arthroscopy can be performed with the patient in the supine or lateral decubitus
position. Supine patient positioning is more common. Correct patient positioning is
essential to establishing safe access to the hip joint.
General anesthesia with muscle relaxation typically is necessary for hip joint distraction
and arthroscopic access; however, some surgeons use spinal anesthesia. The patient is
placed in the supine position on a hip distraction table (Figure 7). Both hip distractors,
using a large perineal post or post-free distraction systems, can be used.7 The authors of
this lesson prefer to use a hip distractor with a large (20 cm), padded perineal post. The
patient’s feet are well padded and then positioned in the traction boots and secured
firmly. The nonsurgical limb is tensioned with gentle traction, with the knee extended
and the hip abducted to 45° to prevent trunk shifting.
Figure 7 Intraoperative photograph shows patient positioning and operating room setup
for hip arthroscopy. (Courtesy of Alan L. Zhang, MD, San Francisco, CA.)
The C-arm should be located on the opposite side of the table from the surgical hip
(Figure 7). A dynamic preoperative fluoroscopic examination is then performed with the
hip in extension and neutral, 30° of internal rotation, and 30° of external rotation. This is
repeated with the hip in 45° of flexion and 90° of flexion with the hip in neutral and in
30° of internal and external rotation.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:21 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000587

Gentle traction is applied to the surgical limb with the knee and hip extended to 0°, the
hip adducted to 0°, and the foot internally rotated 10° to 15°. The anterior superior iliac
spine (ASIS), greater trochanter, and proximal femur should be included in the surgical
field. The hip is then prepared and draped in standard fashion (Figure 8).
Figure 8 Intraoperative photograph shows patient positioning with sterile draping for
hip arthroscopy. (Courtesy of Alan L. Zhang, MD, San Francisco, CA.)
Hip Distraction and Establishing Portals
The safe zone is lateral to a longitudinal line drawn distally from the ASIS. The femoral
neurovascular bundle lies medial to the ASIS.
Air arthrography is used to vent the joint and allow for hip distraction.
The incision for the anterolateral portal is located at the anterosuperior border of the greater
trochanter. This correlates to 12-o’clock position on the intra-articular clockface.
The modified mid-anterior portal (MMAP) is located one fingerbreadth distal and two
fingerbreadths medial to the anterolateral portal (2-o’clock position).
The surgeon should use a 70° arthroscope and keep the water off until both portals are
established.
A combination of direct arthroscopic visualization and fluoroscopic guidance are useful to
ensure safe portal placement without iatrogenic damage.

9/3/26, 4:21 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000587

Surface Landmarks

Surface Landmarks
After the surgical time-out, surface landmarks are drawn, including the ASIS and the
greater trochanter (Figure 9). Landmarks may be drawn before hip distraction but
should be confirmed after hip distraction because they may move. A vertical line is
drawn down the thigh from the ASIS, indicating the danger zone (femoral neurovascular
structures lie medial to the ASIS). Surgeons must remain lateral to this vertical line at all
times during hip joint access. The anterolateral portal is located at the anterosuperior
corner of the greater trochanter, and the MMAP is located approximately one
fingerbreadth distal and two fingerbreadths medial to the anterolateral portal (Figure 9).
Figure 9 Intraoperative photograph of a left hip shows surface landmarks and portals
hip arthroscopy. AL = anterolateral portal, ASIS = anterior superior iliac spine, DALA =
distal anterolateral accessory portal, MMAP = modified mid-anterior portal, PALA =
proximal anterolateral accessory portal, PL = posterolateral portal. (Courtesy of Alan L.
Zhang, MD, San Francisco, CA.)
Air Arthrography and Hip Distraction

Air Arthrography and Hip Distraction

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000587

Fluoroscopy is used to localize the hip joint, and a 16-gauge metal spinal needle
is used to perform air arthrography of the hip joint (Figure 10 and Figure 11).8
Air arthrography neutralizes the normal negative pressure of the joint and
allows access to the hip joint without the need for excessive traction.9 The
needle should be aimed at the femoral neck, which is intra-capsular. (Figure 10).
Then, 25 cc of air is injected, and the air arthrography is confirmed by
fluoroscopy (Figure 11). The needle is then left in the capsule to vent the joint as
the hip is distracted with fine traction. The goal is to have at least 10 mm of joint
space for safe access. Fluoroscopy is assessed to determine if adequate
distraction has been attained. If necessary, additional turns of fine traction can
be applied.
Figure 10 Fluoroscopic image of a hip shows a spinal needle placed
intracapsular before air arthrogram. (Courtesy of Alan L. Zhang, MD, San
Francisco, CA.)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:21 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000587

Figure 11 Fluoroscopic image of a right hip shows air arthrography. (Courtesy of
Alan L. Zhang, MD, San Francisco, CA.)
Portals

Portals
The anterolateral portal is established first under fluoroscopic guidance. The
spinal needle is positioned to enter the hip joint just proximal to the femoral
head, with the angle of the needle matching the angle of the sourcil. The goal is
to have the anterolateral portal enter the hip capsule at the 12-o’clock position
between the femoral head cartilage and the acetabular labrum. If the
anterolateral portal is too proximal, the portal may be within the labrum. If the
anterolateral portal is too distal, iatrogenic damage to femoral head cartilage
may occur.
The center stylet from the needle is removed, and the nitinol guidewire is placed
(Figure 12). If the anterolateral portal is in the correct position, the nitinol wire
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:21 PM
AAOS | Hip Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000587
12/28

should contact the back of the cotyloid fossa. If the nitinol wire stops short, the
portal is too anterior or too posterior.
Figure 12 Fluoroscopic image of a hip shows establishment of the anterolateral
portal with a nitinol guidewire through the spinal needle. (Courtesy of Alan L.
Zhang, MD, San Francisco, CA.)
A 1 cm longitudinal incision is made in the skin centered on the nitinol wire. The
portal is then dilated, and the arthroscopic cannula is placed over the guidewire.
Entering the joint capsule is felt as a loss of resistance sensation. The 70°
arthroscope is connected. The water is kept off at this point because inflow into
the joint without an outflow portal may obscure visualization. The scope is
oriented so the labrum is proximal and the femoral head is distal. Surgeons
should view posteriorly to ensure that the anterolateral portal is not within the
labrum.
A pink- or red-colored triangle of capsule should be present between the
labrum and the femoral head. Under direct visualization with the arthroscope in
the anterolateral portal and fluoroscopic guidance, triangulation is performed to
establish the MMAP (Figure 13). The spinal needle should enter the joint SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:21 PM
AAOS | Hip Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000587
13/28

approximately 2 cm away from the anterolateral portal, between the femoral
head and labrum and directly under the tip of the arthroscope on fluoroscopy
(Figure 14).
At this point, the arthroscope is switched to the MMAP portal. The surgeon
should look back toward the anterolateral portal to assess its position. The
portal should be in the red or pink capsular tissue between the labrum and the
femoral head. If appropriate, the capsulotomy can then be performed.
Other portals that may be used include the direct anterior portal (at the
intersection of a line drawn distally from the ASIS and a line drawn transversely
from the top of the greater trochanter) for access to the anterior labrum, the
distal anterolateral accessory portal for suture anchor placement higher on the
acetabular rim, the posterolateral portal for access to the posterior labrum and
the acetabular fossa, and the proximal anterolateral accessory portal for a
distally directed portal track that can be used for femoroplasty.
Figure 13 Arthroscopic image of a hip with the arthroscope in the anterolateral
portal. The femoral head is on the left of the image, and labrum and
acetabulum are on the right of the image. The spinal needle is used to localize
the modified mid-anterior portal. (Courtesy of Alan L. Zhang, MD, San Francisco,
CA.)

Hip Arthroscopy Technique
The hip joint is accessed via capsulotomy.
The three most common types of capsulotomies are periportal, interportal, and T-
capsulotomy.
Diagnostic arthroscopy includes assessment of the femoral head cartilage, acetabular
cartilage, labrum, and chondrolabral junction.
After the intra-articular, or central compartment, pathology is addressed, surgeons should
ensure the hip suction seal is intact as traction is released.
Peripheral compartment pathology includes cam impingement, which is managed via
femoroplasty.
Capsulotomy Types
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:21 PM
AAOS | Hip Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000587
15/28


Capsulotomy Types
Accessing the hip joint requires a capsulotomy. Three types of capsulotomies are
commonly used: periportal, interportal, and T-capsulotomy10 (Figure 15). The periportal
capsulotomy involves dilating the anterolateral and MMAP portals.11,12 The interportal
capsulotomy connects the anterolateral and MMAP portals. The T-capsulotomy is an
interportal capsulotomy with an additional vertical limb extending down the femoral
neck. The capsulotomy can be performed with the use of a shaver, a radiofrequency
ablation device, or an arthroscopic scalpel blade.
The larger the capsulotomy, the wider the field of view and working space; however, the
integrity of the hip capsule is increasingly recognized as important to hip function and
stability,10 and a shift toward routine capsular closure, especially for a larger
capsulotomy, has been observed.
Figure 15 Illustrations of a hip show the types of capsulotomies (from left to right):
periportal, interportal, and T-capsulotomy. (Reproduced with permission from Nho SJ,
Beck EC, Kunze KN, Okoroha K, Suppauksorn S: Contemporary management of the hip
capsule during arthroscopic hip preservation surgery. Curr Rev Musculoskelet Med
2019;12[3]:260-270.)

Diagnostic Arthroscopy/Zones
Diagnostic arthroscopy of the central compartment is performed with the arthroscope in the
anterolateral portal and a probe in the MMAP (Figures 16-19; Video 1). The following
structures are assessed, and any abnormalities are documented:
Femoral head cartilage
Acetabular cartilage
Labrum
Chondrolabral junction
Figure 16 Arthroscopic image of a left hip undergoing diagnostic arthroscopy (viewing from
anterolateral portal) shows intact femoral head cartilage. (Courtesy of Alan L. Zhang, MD, San
Francisco, CA.)

pathology of the femoral head and the acetabulum in a concise and reproducible

Articular cartilage injuries to the acetabulum and femur also have been described by
Beck et al14 (Table 2).

Central compartment pathology is addressed as indicated, including via acetabuloplasty
or pincer resection, labral repair, chondroplasty, and removal of loose bodies.
After intra-articular work is completed, traction is removed, and the peripheral
compartment is evaluated. The hip suction seal should be evaluated under direct
visualization as traction is removed. The hip can be flexed to 45° to remove tension from
the capsule and aid in visualization. At this point, cam resection can be performed in
patients with femoroacetabular impingement syndrome.
Depending on the type of capsulotomy performed, surgeon preference, and patient
factors, capsular closure has been increasingly used in recent years to restore normal
capsule anatomy.10 This can be performed with the use of various suture shuttling
devices or self-capturing suture passing devices.
Postoperative Management
Postoperatively, patients are flatfoot–weight bearing on crutches for 2 to 3 weeks, with range
of motion limited to 90° of hip flexion, 0° of hip extension, and neutral rotation.
Strengthening begins with gluteal and core isometrics and gradually progresses.
Range of motion is restored and walking and bicycling endurance are increased between 6 and
12 weeks postoperatively.
Return to running progression begins at 3 months postoperatively.
Participation in contact sports occurs approximately 6 months postoperatively.

Postoperative Management
Hip arthroscopy generally is performed as an outpatient surgical procedure. Patients are
flatfoot–weight bearing on crutches for 2 to 3 weeks postoperatively. Physical therapy is
initiated approximately 7 days postoperatively to work on decreasing inflammation and
optimizing pain control and for gentle range of motion. Range of motion is restricted to
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:21 PM
AAOS | Hip Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000587
21/28

less than 90° of hip flexion, no more than 0° of hip extension, and no more than 10° of
hip external rotation for the first 6 weeks postoperatively. The patient begins riding an
upright stationary bike without resistance 7 to 10 days postoperatively, focusing on using
the well leg initially and then adding the surgical limb for pedaling. Strengthening begins
with core and gluteal isometrics and gradually progresses each week.
Goals include normalizing gait by 6 weeks postoperatively. At 6 to 12 weeks
postoperatively, normal range of motion is gradually attained, walking endurance is
increased, and patients are progressed to elliptical and freestyle-kick swimming.
A running progression program is initiated at 3 months postoperatively. A stable single-
leg squat may indicate a patient’s readiness to begin running. Return to contact sports
occurs approximately 6 months postoperatively.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Common pitfalls and pearls for preventing them include the following:
Each step of hip arthroscopy is predicated on properly completing the prior step. Ensure
each step is performed well before moving on.
Proper patient positioning and setup are keys to access.
Heel slippage may result in loss of traction and prevent access to the hip joint. Ensure the
patient’s heels are secure, especially with the strap over the ankle and all the way down
with the foot flat into the traction boots.
Inform the anesthesia team of need for muscle relaxation before induction. Assess the
degree of muscle relaxation with the anesthesia team if hip distraction is inadequate.
Establishing portals
Anterolateral portal is within the labrum.
A veil of tissue in the superior half of the arthroscopic view may indicate being within the
labrum and too proximal. If this is the case, start over and correct the anterolateral portal
position before proceeding, or, if adequate visualization exists, correct the anterolateral
portal position after the MMAP has been established.
Anterolateral portal creation causing iatrogenic damage to femoral head
Ensure at least 10 mm of joint distraction.

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000587
22/28

Hard resistance in placing the spinal needle, dilator, or cannula may indicate touching
cartilage.
Use fluoroscopy to ensure correct trajectory, and lever the dilator and cannula away from
the femoral head cartilage.
MMAP
Use a combination of direct visualization and fluoroscopy to establish the MMAP. Aim the
spinal needle tip near the arthroscope on fluoroscopy.
The MMAP should be at the 2-o’clock position. If it is too anterior (appears in the far
distance to your anterolateral portal), then reposition the spinal needle closer to the
anterolateral portal. Coming all the way out of skin and then replacing the spinal needle is
helpful to create a new trajectory.
Diagnostic arthroscopy
Poor visualization
Check fluoroscopic images to ensure the arthroscope is properly positioned in the joint
(not too deep or superficial).
Ensure water is connected, adequate water is remaining, and outflow is open.
A shaver can be used to carefully remove debris and improve the view if some
visualization is present to prevent iatrogenic shaver damage.
Increase the pump pressure temporarily to improve visualization. Decrease the pump
pressure if visualization is restored to prevent excessive swelling.
Turn the arthroscopic eye to view all zones.
Excessive traction time
Assess positioning and ability to obtain fluoroscopic images before applying traction.
Ask the circulating nurse to document traction time in a visible location (ie, whiteboard in
the operating room) and announce traction time in 30-minute increments. The goal is less
than 2 hours of traction time.
If traction time approaches 2 hours, then release traction for 15 to 20 minutes and switch
to peripheral compartment work in the meantime.
Complications
Hip arthroscopy is technically challenging.
Complications include residual impingement, iatrogenic chondrolabral injury, traction-related
complications (eg, pudendal nerve neuropraxia), lateral femoral cutaneous nerve palsy,

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000587
23/28

heterotopic bone formation, instability, femoral neck fracture from excessive resection, and
abdominal/thigh compartment syndrome.

Complications
Hip arthroscopy is a technically challenging procedure. Several complications have been
reported.
In a systematic review, Harris et al15 reported that the most common complication
during hip arthroscopy was iatrogenic chondrolabral injury. This can be minimized via
careful portal positioning and ensuring correct placement of anchors.
If using a perineal post for distraction, the perineal and pudendal nerves can be injured
from compression and prolonged traction time. A study of 3,405 hip arthroscopy
procedures reported a 1.8% risk of pudendal nerve injury.16 All cases were transient
neuropraxias and the patients recovered within 3 months. Post-free distraction tables
have been developed and proposed as a method to avoid these complications, using
Trendelenburg positioning instead.7
Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve palsy related to mid-anterior portal placement has
been reported in the literature and was reported in 17.8% of patients in a study.17
Surgeons must incise just the skin and avoid diving into the subcutaneous tissue during
skin incision to minimize the risk of lateral femoral cutaneous nerve palsy.17,18
Abdominal compartment syndrome is a rare but devastating complication of hip
arthroscopy.19-25 Mainly case reports are available in the literature; therefore, the exact
rate of occurrence is difficult to determine. Risk factors for development of abdominal
compartment syndrome include traction time for more than 2 hours, excessive
extracapsular dissection, and dissection near the iliopsoas (ie, for iliopsoas tenotomy)
because fluid can track proximally along the iliopsoas and into the retroperitoneal space
and, potentially, the intraperitoneal space.19 Signs of abdominal compartment
syndrome include hemodynamic instability (hypotension, cardiac arrhythmias, cardiac
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:21 PM
AAOS | Hip Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000587
24/28

arrest), hypothermia, hypoxia, increased peak pressures, and abdominal distension and
rigidity and may progress to multisystem organ failure and death.19,20 Abdominal
compartment syndrome is a life-threatening emergency. If encountered, hip arthroscopy
should be aborted, and urgent abdominal fasciotomy should be performed.23
Other intraoperative complications include injury to neurovascular structures, such as
the femoral neurovascular bundle,26 and inadequate osseous resection leading to
residual impingement and the need for revision surgery.27 Postoperative complications
may include heterotopic ossification (5% to 15%), instability/microinstability, infection,
venous thromboembolism, osteonecrosis of the femoral head, adhesion formation, and
femoral neck fracture from excessive resection.26
